meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The power of imagination makes us infinite'?
meta.ogDescription: A real John Muir line — from his 1 Sept 1875 journal, printed in John of the Mountains (1938), p. 226. Usually quoted sourceless and lightly trimmed.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1838–1914 · Scottish-American naturalist & founder of the Sierra Club
answer.sourceLine: Genuine. Muir wrote it in his mountain journal on 1 September 1875; the full sentence — “Indeed, the power of imagination makes us infinite” — was first published in John of the Mountains (1938), p. 226. The popular version simply drops the opening “Indeed.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Indeed, the power of imagination makes us infinite.”
John of the Mountains: The Unpublished Journals of John Muir

source.excerpt: How infinitely superior to our physical senses are those of the mind! … Imagination is usually regarded as a synonym for the unreal. Yet is true imagination healthful and real, no more likely to mislead than the coarser senses. Indeed, the power of imagination makes us infinite.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section prints the full sentence and cites it to John of the Mountains (1938), p. 226, dated 1 September 1875.
The Sierra Club John Muir Exhibit independently lists the quote with the same source and page.
The journals were compiled and edited by Linnie Marsh Wolfe and issued by Houghton Mifflin in 1938 for Muir’s centenary, 24 years after his death.
source.excerptNote: The line closes a journal meditation on the “spiritual eye” — Muir’s argument that the mind, through imagination, perceives more of nature than the physical senses can. It is a claim about perception, not the generic pep-talk it is usually repackaged as.
source.rightsHolder: Houghton Mifflin (1938 first edition); John Muir estate / Muir-Hanna Trust; reprinted 1979 by University of Wisconsin Press
source.rightsNote: The thought is Muir’s 1875 journal writing, but this text was first published in 1938 in John of the Mountains (Houghton Mifflin), edited by Linnie Marsh Wolfe — a 1938 U.S. publication remains under copyright (it enters the public domain on 1 January 2034). Muir’s books issued in his lifetime are public-domain, but this specific posthumously-published journal edition is not.

author.heading: About John Muir
author.metaLine: 1838–1914 · Scottish-American naturalist, writer & founder of the Sierra Club
author.bio: John Muir (1838–1914) was a Scottish-born American naturalist, essayist and wilderness advocate often called the “Father of the National Parks.” His writing on the Sierra Nevada helped protect Yosemite and Sequoia, and in 1892 he co-founded the Sierra Club. Much of his most vivid observation survives in field journals published only decades after his death.

misattribution.heading: The credit is right — the sourcing isn’t
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a feel-good line pinned to a famous naturalist, this one is authentically Muir. What’s wrong is how it travels: almost always sourceless, lightly trimmed, and stripped of what Muir actually meant.

items.why: BrainyQuote, Goodreads and AZQuotes all reproduce the line with no book, journal or date — the exact gap this page fills.

Muir’s sentence begins “Indeed, the power of imagination…” and closes a passage about the “spiritual eye” out-perceiving the senses; the standalone slogan drops the opening word and the argument around it, per the full text on Wikiquote.

misattribution.truthLine: It really is John Muir — from his journal of 1 September 1875, published in John of the Mountains (1938), p. 226.

context.heading: What Muir actually meant
lead: Muir jotted the line in the Sierra Nevada in 1875, not as motivation but as epistemology. The surrounding entry argues that the “spiritual eye” of the mind perceives what the senses miss — rivers of air, the vibration of every pine needle, “the sound of stars in circulation like particles in the blood.”
For Muir, imagination wasn’t escapism (“usually regarded as a synonym for the unreal”) but a truer instrument of perception — and that is what he meant by it making us “infinite.”
context.pull: “True imagination… no more likely to mislead than the coarser senses.”
